mcqs.question: Why does a message only leave the queue's unacked set when the queue receives an Acknowledgement, rather than the moment a consumer receives it?
options: Because Producers require a confirmation before they can publish another message
Because if delivery alone removed a message and the consumer then crashed before finishing, the message would be lost with no record that it needs retrying
Because ConsumerGroups cannot track which consumer received which message otherwise
Because messages are immutable and cannot be marked as delivered
mcqs.explanation: Treating 'delivered' as 'done' throws away the queue's ability to detect and recover from a consumer that fails mid-processing — the entire at-least-once guarantee depends on the message staying tracked until it's explicitly acked. This has nothing to do with producers needing confirmation, ConsumerGroup bookkeeping, or message mutability.

mcqs.question: A consumer finishes processing a message but crashes right before sending the ack. What does the queue's ack-timeout mechanism do, and why does this make the guarantee at-least-once rather than exactly-once?
options: The queue permanently discards the message since it can't confirm success
The queue extends the ack timeout indefinitely until the consumer restarts

The queue requeues the message after the timeout, and since it can't distinguish 'finished but didn't ack' from 'crashed before finishing,' the message may be processed again — producing a duplicate rather than a loss
The queue automatically deduplicates the message using its timestamp
mcqs.explanation: The queue can only observe the absence of an ack, not why it's absent, so it has to assume the safer case and requeue — which is exactly what makes duplicate processing possible and the guarantee at-least-once, not exactly-once. It doesn't discard the message, doesn't extend the timeout indefinitely, and has no built-in deduplication by timestamp.

mcqs.question: Why do most production systems achieve what they call 'exactly-once' behavior by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers, rather than building true exactly-once delivery into the queue?
options: True exactly-once delivery is impossible in any distributed or concurrent system
At-least-once delivery cannot be combined with idempotency in practice

True exactly-once delivery at the transport layer requires expensive coordination (like transactional guarantees between queue and consumer state), while at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer achieves the same practical outcome far more cheaply
Idempotent consumers eliminate the need for acknowledgements entirely
mcqs.explanation: The pragmatic combination avoids paying for strong transactional guarantees at the transport layer by pushing duplicate-safety into the consumer, which is usually far cheaper to build. Exactly-once isn't strictly impossible, just expensive; at-least-once and idempotency compose well together (that's the whole point); and idempotent consumers still need acks to know what's been delivered.

mcqs.question: Why do most message queue designs offer per-partition ordering instead of a single global order across all messages?
options: Global ordering requires a single consumer processing one message at a time, capping throughput; per-partition ordering lets unrelated messages (e.g. different users' events) be consumed in parallel while still ordering what actually needs it
Per-partition ordering is required because queues cannot guarantee any ordering at all otherwise
Global ordering is impossible to implement in any message queue
Partitions exist only to support multiple producers, not for ordering
mcqs.explanation: The trade is explicitly about throughput: global order forces serialization, while grouping by key confines the ordering guarantee to where it usually matters (within one entity's events) and frees unrelated partitions to run in parallel. Global ordering is possible, just expensive; queues can guarantee ordering, just at different scopes; and partitions serve ordering and parallelism together, not only multi-producer support.

mcqs.question: A consumer acks a message immediately after pulling it off the queue, before actually processing it, to avoid hitting the ack timeout. What guarantee does this silently downgrade the system to?
options: Exactly-once, since the message is guaranteed to be acked
At-most-once — if the consumer crashes during processing, the message is already acked and permanently lost, with no retry
Global ordering, since acking early changes message order
It has no effect on delivery guarantees, only on latency
mcqs.explanation: Acking before processing completes removes the message from the in-flight set for good — a crash afterward means the work never happens and nothing retries it, which is exactly the at-most-once behavior the ack-timeout design was meant to avoid. It doesn't produce exactly-once (the opposite direction), has nothing to do with ordering, and is a correctness issue, not just a latency one.
